```js
function _getParentBlockRoot(uint64 timestamp) internal view returns (bytes32) {
    //@audit `abi.encode` returns bytes not bytes32!!!
    (bool success, bytes memory result) = Constants.BEACON_ROOTS_ADDRESS.staticcall(abi.encode(timestamp)); 
    ...
}
```

> 8.1.3 . Due to the points above, smart contract developers might perform a low-level call in the respective smart contract language. That low-level call generally does not perform checks, such as sufficient return data. Hence, smart contracts performing such a low-level call should check that the RETURNDATASIZE == 32 using the features of the respective language.

However in the code, result is directly casted to `bytes32` without prior check of `RETURNDATASIZE`:
```js
...
if (success && result.length > 0) {
    return abi.decode(result, (bytes32));
} else {
    revert BeaconRootFetchError();
```

# Vulnerability details

## Description 

In `Core.sol`, the function `registerDSS()` is designed to register a Decentralized Staking System (DSS) with the platform. Currently, this function checks if the caller is a smart contract by checking the code length at the caller's address. However, this method is not foolproof. With the widespread use of smart contracts and multisig wallets, it’s possible for malicious attacker to exploit this simple check, registering unauthorized DSS instances and potentially compromising the system’s integrity.

## Code

```solidity
function registerDSS(uint256 maxSlashablePercentageWad) external {
        IDSS dss = IDSS(msg.sender);
        if (!address(dss).isSmartContract()) revert NotSmartContract();
        _self().setDSSMaxSlashablePercentageWad(dss, maxSlashablePercentageWad);
        emit DSSRegistered(msg.sender, maxSlashablePercentageWad);
    }
```

## Impact

This vulnerability could allow unauthorized entities to register as DSS, potentially leading to security breaches or manipulation within the system. Malicious actors could exploit this loophole.

## Recommendation

To enhance security and ensure only legitimate DSS instances can register,the system should check for the implementation of a specific interface that bona fide DSS contracts would support. This approach adds an extra layer of validation, helping to confirm the identity and legitimacy of the caller.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function allows an operator to either stake or unstake a vault to/from a DSS (Decentralized Staking System). The StakeUpdateRequest struct includes a boolean field, toStake, which indicates whether the operator intends to stake (true) or unstake (false) the vault.

Within the `requestUpdateVaultStakeInDSS` function, the callHookIfInterfaceImplemented is invoked to handle hooks if implemented by the DSS. One of the parameters for this function, ignoreFailure, is set to the negation of `requestStakeUpdate.toStake`

```javascript
 ignoreFailure: !requestStakeUpdate.toStake
```

This means that if the operation is a stake (toStake is true), ignoreFailure is set to false, and if the operation is an unstake (toStake is false), ignoreFailure is set to true.
Inconsistent Behavior: Depending on the implementation of the hook in the DSS, this could lead to inconsistent behavior where the hook call may fail silently during unstaking but not during staking. This might not be the intended functionality and can cause logical errors or unintended side effects.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L82
Stake Request:
When requestStakeUpdate.toStake is true, ignoreFailure is set to false.
The hook call will not ignore failures, meaning any failure during the staking hook execution will propagate.
```javascript 
ignoreFailure: !requestStakeUpdate.toStake  // translates to ignoreFailure: false
```
Unstake Request:

When requestStakeUpdate.toStake is false, ignoreFailure is set to true.
The hook call will ignore failures, meaning any failure during the unstaking hook execution will be ignored.
```javascript
ignoreFailure: !requestStakeUpdate.toStake  // translates to ignoreFailure: true

 ```

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure the ignoreFailure parameter aligns with the intended functionality of the protocol. If failures should not be ignored during either operation, remove the negation. or vice versa
```javascript 
ignoreFailure: false

```

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

The HookLib.sol is responsible for calling hooks on the DSS contract. Before calling one, it uses the ERC165 to validate that the DSS contract supports the function selector that will be called as a hook. However, the implementation does not follow Ethereum's [ERC165 standard.](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-165)

## Vulnerability Details

In the details of the Karak audit page on CodeArena, it states that:
```
EIP compliance checklist
- DSS contract should comply with ERC-165.
```

The ERC165 standard states that the call to the supportsInterface method should be a `STATICCALL` for security, ensuring that the call won't modify the state. However, in the current implementation in HookLib.sol, the performLowLevelCallAndLimitReturnData uses `CALL` instead of `STATICCALL`.

```solidity
    function performLowLevelCallAndLimitReturnData(address target, bytes memory data, uint256 gasLimit)
        internal
        returns (bool success, bytes32 returnVal)
    {
        bytes32[1] memory returnData;

        assembly {
            // pointer(data) + 0x20 is where actual data is available
            // pointer(data) contains the size of the data in bytes
            // returnData is where the return value is written to
            // we limit size of return value to 32 bytes (same as the size of `returnData` above)
            success :=
 @>>            call(
                    gasLimit, // gas available to the inner call
                    target, // address of contract being called
                    0, // ETH (denominated in WEI) being transferred in this call
                    add(data, 0x20), // Pointer to actual data (i.e. 32 bytes offset from `data`)
                    mload(data), // Size of actual data (i.e. the value stored in the first 32 bytes at `data`)
                    returnData, // Free pointer as a buffer for the inner call to write the return value
                    32 // 32 bytes size limit for the return value
                )
        }
        returnVal = returnData[0];
    }
```

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommendations

Comply to ERC-165 by using `STATICCALL` instead of `CALL`

If exploited, this overflow could lead to incorrect balance calculations, potentially allowing for manipulation of validator balances. In a proof-of-stake system, this could have significant consequences for validator rewards, slashing, and overall system integrity.

To mitigate this risk, explicitly cast `validatorIndex` to `uint256` before performing the calculation:

```solidity
uint256 bitShiftAmount = (uint256(validatorIndex) % 4) * 64;
```

This explicit cast ensures that even if `validatorIndex` somehow contains a value larger than intended, the calculation will be performed correctly within the `uint256` range.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/NativeVaultLib.sol#L169


# Vulnerability details

## Impact


## Proof of Concept
When the user calls the validateWithdrawalCredentials function, their balance only increases by 32 ETH, even if the validator has more than 32 ETH. This is because the function uses getEffectiveBalanceWei, which returns a maximum of 32 ETH.

```solidity
uint256 restakedBalanceWei = BeaconProofs.getEffectiveBalanceWei(validatorFieldsProof.validatorFields);
        BeaconProofs.validateValidatorProof(
            validatorFieldsProof.validatorProof.validatorIndex,
            validatorFieldsProof.validatorFields,
            validatorFieldsProof.validatorProof.proof,
            beaconStateRoot
        );

        validatorDetails.status = NativeVaultLib.ValidatorStatus.ACTIVE;
        validatorDetails.validatorIndex = validatorFieldsProof.validatorProof.validatorIndex;
        validatorDetails.lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp = updateTimestamp;
        validatorDetails.restakedBalanceWei = restakedBalanceWei;
        self.ownerToNode[nodeOwner].validatorPubkeyHashToDetails[validatorPubkeyHash] = validatorDetails;
        self.ownerToNode[nodeOwner].activeValidatorCount++;

        emit RestakedValidator(
            nodeOwner,
            self.ownerToNode[nodeOwner].nodeAddress,
            validatorFieldsProof.validatorProof.validatorIndex,
            updateTimestamp,
            restakedBalanceWei
        );
        return restakedBalanceWei;
```

This can cause problems when the user wants to withdraw from the native vault. 

Suppose a user wants to withdraw and calls the validateSnapshotProofs function after starting a snapshot. At that time, the user's native node balance will be 64 ETH, and they can withdraw their funds using the finishWithdrawal function. However, if slashing occurs before the withdrawal, the user will face penalties based on their 64 ETH, not 32 ETH. This is unfair as the user earns DSS rewards based on their vault shares, which are 32 ETH when the user staked.

POC:


Let's consider native vaults with the following values:
- totalSupply: 100e18
- totalAsset: 100e18

When a user stakes, their shares will be 32e18, and they will receive DSS rewards according to their 32e18 shares. 

If the user withdraws from the validator and calls the validateSnapshotProofs function, the vault's totalSupply will become 132e18, and the totalAsset will become 132e18. Consequently, the user's share will increase to 64e18.

When the vault gets slashed, leading to the totalAsset becoming 122e18, the user calls the finishWithdrawal function and they can only withdraw 59.15e18.

The slash reduced the user's share from 64e18 to 59.15e18, resulting in a loss of 4.85e18.
(64e18 * 122e18 / 132e18 = 59.15e18 ==> 64e18 - 59.15e18 = 4.85e18)

If the user only has 32ETH, their loss will be 3.2e18.
(32e18 * 90e18 / 100e18 = 28.8e18 ==> 32e18 - 28,8e18 = 3.2e18)

Due to the use of getEffectiveBalanceWei, users receive lower rewards and can face higher penalties.
## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider using the validateBalance instead of getEffectiveBalanceWei. When the user stakes, they will have 64 ETH instead of 32 ETH, making everything fair.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Operators could get away without being slashed due to rounding error while calculating `EarmarkedStakes`

## Proof of Concept
The root of cause of this bug is because of two reasons
1. Allowing all ERC20's that means `totalAssets()` function could return a value with 6 decimal places if asset is usdc.
2. The assumption that DSS will provide a wad percentage with 18 decimals

Let's elaborate this
1. We start with `registerDSS` that is responsible for DSS registration by setting the `maxSlashablePercentageWad` provided by the DSS:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L262

As we can see, even though the function is expecting to provide a wad value, which will be let's say 30e18, it does not check if the input value is actually 18 decimal places or not.
Nor, the internal call to `setDSSMaxSlashablePercentageWad` here:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L174-L185

It only checks 2 things with input param. 
a.  should not be zero
b. should be greater than MAX
`This means that if DSS is passing 1 as a value , it will be accepted`

2. Now comes `requestSlashing` where DSS is providing the `slashPercent` in request metadata in an array of vault address and their respective values

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L220-L231

This goes to SlasherLib:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L101

We have a validation function before this 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L59
which checks
a. length mismatch of vault array and slash percent array
b. one more internal call 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L42
that reverts on 0 input and greater than MAX. 

`That means, there's no way to stop if slash percent is not with 18 decimal places.`

Now the call goes to mulDiv via `fetchEarmarkedStakes` where `totalAssets()` in vault is Usdc ( 6 decimals ) and DSS hasn't provided correct 18 decimal places ( let's say 30 instead of 30e18 )
so formula in terms of decimals will become.

```
10(from input value 30)  * 1e6 (usdc)
------------------------------------
          1e18(MAX WAD)
```

This will ultimately round down to 0. Moreover, as long has the numerator value is smaller than 18 decimal places, this value will remain 0. 
Since this value will be used to check the amount of assets to be slashed from vaults via `slashAssets` in `finalizeSlashing`
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L135

We can say that no assets will be slashed in case of any malicious act done by Operators. 

One could argue that this is the DSS's responsibility to provide correct values upon registering and requesting for slash but since DSS service and any operator could become a part of ecosystem we have to make sure that even though DSS's devs should be aware of the difference between normal value and wad, a mistake like this should not penetrate into the system. 

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
A simple check to ensure that the final value after dividing by 1e18 should be greater than 0 in `registerDSS` and `requestSlashing` could mitigate this.

# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The `CoreLib` library incorrectly utilizes the `LibClone.predictDeterministicAddressERC1967BeaconProxy` function during the creation of new vaults. Specifically, the function is provided with `address(this)` as the salt parameter instead of a uniquely generated salt, leading to inaccurate predictions of the new vault's address.

The vulnerability arises in the `createVault` function within the `CoreLib` library. The function aims to predict the address of a new vault using the `LibClone.predictDeterministicAddressERC1967BeaconProxy` function. However, the salt parameter passed to this function is mistakenly set to `address(this)`, which represents the address of the `CoreLib` library itself. This misuse leads to an incorrect prediction of the vault's address, potentially causing the contract to interact with an incorrect or non-existent contract.

## Impact
The contract may attempt to interact with a non-existent or incorrect contract, leading to failed transactions and potential loss of funds.

The `_decreaseBalance` method in the NativeVault contract calls the _beforeWithdraw method, which is responsible for reducing the user's balance by burning the corresponding share and updating the total assets and re-staked ETH. This is because calling an undefined method in Solidity will cause the contract execution to fail, thereby rolling back the entire transaction.
- **Interrupt operation**: Any operation that depends on the `_decreaseBalance` method will fail. For example, user attempts to withdraw, redeem, or other operations involving reducing balances will not be completed. This may cause key functions of the contract to not function properly.

```solidity
}
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Vaults won't be initalized with a underlying token, whose symbol is a type of `bytes32` instead of `string`, as it would lead to a revert.

## Proof of Concept

Although most of the tokens have got a symbol function implemented, it is completely optional therefore any token which doesn't implement it, or has made changes to the function, will still be compliant as per the [EIP](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20#symbol):
> OPTIONAL - This method can be used to improve usability, but interfaces and other contracts MUST NOT expect these values to be present.

Following the contest's readme all ERC20 tokens should be supported by the protocol: 
> Any (all possible ERC20s)

Whenever a new `vault` gets initialized, the underlying token's address, name, decimals and symbol are used in the [initialize](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L51-L71) function. This means that if any of these parameters are not set correctly, a revert will occur, and the `vault` will not be initialized. Such is the case when a token like [MKR](https://etherscan.io/token/0x9f8f72aa9304c8b593d555f12ef6589cc3a579a2#code) or [RING](https://etherscan.io/token/0x9469d013805bffb7d3debe5e7839237e535ec483) is used, where the returned symbol is with type of `bytes32`. The non-string `symbol` won't be converted to a string, causing a revert and preventing the `vault` from being initialized.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

One way to mitigate this issue is to first determine whether the symbol is a `string` or `bytes32` - if it's `bytes32`, the value should be converted to a string and then used for the config of the vault.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
None of the vaults protocol contracts include a __gap variable. Without this variable, it is not possible to add any new variables to the inherited contracts without causing storage slot issues. Specifically, if variables are added to an inherited contract, the storage slots of all subsequent variables in the contract will shift by the number of variables added. Such a shift would likely break the contract

## Proof of Concept
[src/Vault.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/Vault.sol#L29)
[src/NativeVault.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L25)
```solidity
import {Initializable} from "@openzeppelin-upgradeable/proxy/utils/Initializable.sol";  <@

import {Pauser} from "./entities/Pauser.sol";
import {VaultLib} from "./entities/VaultLib.sol";
import {WithdrawLib} from "./entities/Withdraw.sol";

function initialize( <@
    address _owner,
    address _operator,
    address _depositToken,
    string memory _name,
    string memory _symbol,
    bytes memory _extraData
) external initializer {
    _initializeOwner(_owner);
    __Pauser_init();
```

According to above code we can see vaults is upgradeable protocol.

The Vault and NativeVault contract are intended to be used as logic contracts with a proxy, but do not have a __gap variable. This would become problematic if a subsequent version was to inherit one of these contracts. If the derived version were to have storage variables itself and additional storage variables were subsequently added to the inherited contract, a storage collision would occur.


## Tools Used
Foundry
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider appending a __gap variable as the last storage variable to these upgradeable contracts

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
It is impossible to update the validator's balance in future snapshots as the number of active validators for all native nodes will always remain at 0.

## Proof of Concept

Node owners invoke the [`NativeVault::validateWithdrawalCredentials()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L168C2-L204C6) function to add active validators to their native node:

```solidity
for (uint256 i = 0; i < validatorFieldsProofs.length; i++) {
            totalRestakedWei += self.validateWithdrawalCredentials(
                nodeOwner,
                beaconStateRootProof.timestamp,
                beaconStateRootProof.beaconStateRoot,
                validatorFieldsProofs[i]
            );
        }
```

However, after calling [`NativeVault::validateWithdrawalCredentials()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L168C2-L204C6) to add all active validators in the loop above, the function does not increase the node.activeValidatorCount (i.e., the number of active validators in a native node) by the number of newly added validators.
This makes it impossible to update the validator's balance in future snapshots as the number of active validators for all native nodes will always remain at 0.

## Tools Used

Manual review

Increment node.activeValidatorCount by the number of active validators:

```diff

            totalRestakedWei += self.validateWithdrawalCredentials(
                nodeOwner,
                beaconStateRootProof.timestamp,
                beaconStateRootProof.beaconStateRoot,
                validatorFieldsProofs[i]
            );
        }
+        node.activeValidatorCount += validatorFieldsProofs.length;
        _increaseBalance(nodeOwner, totalRestakedWei);
```

In the M-1 of the [Renascence report](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/audits/eth-native-restaking/Renascence%20-%20Karak%20Native%20Restaking%20Audit%20Report.pdf) the following fix was implemented to reset the `withdrawalMap[withdrawalKey]` storage:

```diff
_decreaseBalance(startedWithdrawal.nodeOwner, startedWithdrawal.assets);
        INativeNode(node.nodeAddress).withdraw(startedWithdrawal.to, startedWithdrawal.assets);
        node.withdrawableCreditedNodeETH -= startedWithdrawal.assets;

+        delete self.withdrawalMap[withdrawalKey];
```

# Vulnerability details

The `registerOperatorToDSS()` does not correctly handle this [edge case], leading to unexpected behavior during operator registration. When an operator attempts to register with a DSS that they are already registered with. The current implementation does not check for this scenario, potentially allowing multiple registrations of the same operator to the same DSS.

The `Core` contract manages the registration of operators to various DSS instances. The `registerOperatorToDSS()` function ([lines 97-107](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Core.sol#L97-L107)) is designed to allow operators to register with a DSS, enabling them to allocate assets delegated by stakers, the current implementation fails to properly handle all scenarios, potentially leading to inconsistent state or unintended behavior.

The issue is how the function processes the registration request, particularly in [edge cases](https://prover.certora.com/output/818480/c78dd587baa345b2983a07e64b8476d8?anonymousKey=d63f52f9c10e73adfd759e9c60447fa0f530829e&params=%7B%225%22%3A%7B%22index%22%3A0%2C%22ruleCounterExamples%22%3A%5B%7B%22name%22%3A%22rule_output_2.json%22%2C%22callResolutionSingleFilter%22%3A%22%22%2C%22variablesFilter%22%3A%22%22%2C%22callTraceFilter%22%3A%22%22%2C%22variablesOpenItems%22%3A%5Btrue%2Ctrue%5D%2C%22callTraceCollapsed%22%3Atrue%2C%22rightSidePanelCollapsed%22%3Afalse%2C%22callResolutionSingleCollapsed%22%3Atrue%2C%22viewStorage%22%3Atrue%2C%22expandedArray%22%3A%2240-10-10-1-18-1-1-1-124-1-1-139%22%2C%22orderVars%22%3A%5B%22%22%2C%22%22%2C0%5D%2C%22orderParams%22%3A%5B%22%22%2C%22%22%2C0%5D%2C%22scrollPosition%22%3A%7B%22top%22%3A178.13333129882812%2C%22left%22%3A0%7D%2C%22currentPoint%22%3A0%2C%22childrenIds%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22parentIds%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22trackingOnly%22%3Afalse%2C%22singleCallResolutionOpen%22%3A%5B%5D%7D%5D%7D%7D&generalState=%7B%22fileViewOpen%22%3Atrue%2C%22fileViewCollapsed%22%3Atrue%2C%22mainTreeViewCollapsed%22%3Atrue%2C%22callTraceClosed%22%3Afalse%2C%22mainSideNavItem%22%3A%22rules%22%2C%22globalResSelected%22%3Afalse%2C%22isSideBarCollapsed%22%3Afalse%2C%22isRightSideBarCollapsed%22%3Afalse%2C%22selectedFile%22%3A%7B%22path%22%3A%22.certora_sources%2FregisterOperatorToDSS.spec%22%2C%22name%22%3A%22registerOperatorToDSS.spec%22%2C%22uiID%22%3A%22f9af06%22%7D%2C%22fileViewFilter%22%3A%22%22%2C%22mainTreeViewFilter%22%3A%22%22%2C%22contractsFilter%22%3A%22%22%2C%22globalCallResolutionFilter%22%3A%22%22%2C%22currentRuleUiId%22%3A5%2C%22counterExamplePos%22%3A1%2C%22expandedKeysState%22%3A%225-10-1-1-03-1-05-1-1-1-1-1%22%2C%22expandedFilesState%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22outlinedfilterShared%22%3A%22000000000%22%7D) that have been initially considered. This could result in operators being incorrectly registered or failing to register when they should be able to.

## Impact

The incorrect handling of edge cases in the `registerOperatorToDSS()` function could lead to:

1. Operators being unable to register with certain DSS instances when they should be allowed to.
2. Inconsistent state between the Core contract and the DSS regarding operator registration.
3. Potential loss of functionality for affected operators, as they may be unable to allocate assets or participate in the protocol as intended.

These issues could undermine the reliability and functionality of the operator registration process, potentially affecting the overall stability and trustworthiness of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

The function should include a check to prevent an operator from registering with a DSS they are already registered with, ensuring the integrity of the registration process.

1. An operator attempts to register with a DSS using `registerOperatorToDSS()`.
2. The function checks if the DSS is registered using `self.isDSSRegistered(dss)`.
3. Due to the edge case not being properly handled, the function fails to register the operator or registers them incorrectly.
4. The operator is now in an inconsistent state, unable to properly interact with the DSS or allocate assets.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```solidity
function registerOperatorToDSS(IDSS dss, bytes memory registrationHookData)
    external
    whenFunctionNotPaused(Constants.PAUSE_CORE_REGISTER_TO_DSS)
    nonReentrant
{
    address operator = msg.sender;
    CoreLib.Storage storage self = _self();
    if (!self.isDSSRegistered(dss)) revert DSSNotRegistered();
    
    // Add additional checks here
    if (self.isOperatorRegisteredToDSS(operator, dss)) revert OperatorAlreadyRegistered();
    
    // Proceed with registration
    self.registerOperatorToDSS(dss, operator, registrationHookData);
    emit RegisteredOperatorToDSS(operator, address(dss));
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L97-L100


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`DSS`s must conform to ERC165 interface call and in doing so enables hooks that are used by the karak protocol for various operations.

By reverting on ERC165 operations a DSS can prevent karak protocol operations like slashing, operator removal, or vault validation from working even when karak protocol could safely ignore this hooks reverting. 


## Proof of Concept

The function `callHookIfInterfaceImplemented` should not revert when `ignoreFailure` is passed as true.
But on the following line a DSS can make a non reverting call revert (as `InterfaceNotSupported()`) by removing the supported of the ERC165 interface during a hook call.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L97-L100

This can affect operation when involving slashing:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L94

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L126

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L153

or when unregister operator from a DSS is called:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L181

and when updating or validating vault stakes:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L61

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/Operator.sol#L111

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

When `ignoreFailure` is set to true do not revert in case of a ERC165 error:

```diff
    function callHookIfInterfaceImplemented(
        IERC165 dss,
        bytes memory data,
        bytes4 interfaceId,
        bool ignoreFailure,
        uint32 hookCallGasLimit,
        uint32 supportsInterfaceGasLimit,
        uint32 hookGasBuffer
    ) internal returns (bool) {
        ...

-        if (!success || result == bytes32(0)) {
+        if (!ignoreFailure && (!success || result == bytes32(0))) {
            // Either call failed or interface isn't implemented
            emit InterfaceNotSupported();
            return false;
        }
        ...
    }
}
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

All assets which are meant to be slashed by DSS can be misused by the rogue or compromised Manager. In addition, attacker which has previously compromised Manager EOA and has this capability can use intentionally to break security rules/invariants of particular DSS. 

## Proof of Concept

In [SlasherLib.finalizeSlashing()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/SlasherLib.sol#L135..L138) slashingHandler for particular asset is dynamically retrieved and passed to [Vault.slashAssets()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/Vault.sol#L193..L205) function. Vault fully trusts provided slashingHandler contract and approves for transfer designated amount meant to be slashed.

However, account with Manager role, which can be EOA as stated by the client, may change at any point slashingHandler for any asset through Core.allowlistAssets() and CoreLib.allowlistAssets(). As a result, compromised Manager EOA may update trusted slashingHandler implementation for popular asset with contract which would drain and redirect assets meant to be slashed. In addition, attacker (compromised manager) may trigger this operation by directly calling Core.finalizeSlashing()

- Do not allow slashing handler to be changed, or enforce timelocked updates for any slashing handler change.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/entities/CoreLib.sol#L132-L145
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/main/src/NativeVault.sol#L83-L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Malicious operators may deploy the native vaults with their own native node implementation addresses. With these customized native nodes, they can run bad actions, such as stealing node owners' withdrawn ETHs that must be sent to the owners' intended addresses.

## Proof of Concept

When creating a native vault, the implementation address of Native Node is provided through the `extraData` parameter.

Neither `CoreLib::deployVaults()` nor `CoreLib::createVault()` conduct a whitelist validation of the native node implementation, and any contract can be a logic contract address of the deployed native node proxy.

As being an operator doesn't require owner's approval, anybody can be an operator without any problem.

Consequently, a malicious operator may create a native vault with a bad native node implementation. Or after creating a vault with a normal node implementation, he may change it to malicious code later through the `NativeVault::changeNodeImplementation()` function.

### PoC Test

To prove this, I modified the `nativeVault.t.sol` by changing line 85 from
```solidity
    address nativeNodeImpl = address(new NativeNode());
```
to
```solidity
    address nativeNodeImpl = address(0xdeadbeaf);
```

And added the below new test case:
```solidity
    function test_createNode_badImpl(address nodeOwner) public {
        assertEq(nativeVault.implementation(), address(0xdeadbeef));
    }

```

Here's logs of successful running of the test case:
```
Ran 1 test for test/nativeRestaking/nativeVault.t.sol:NativeVaultTest
[PASS] test_createNode_badImpl(address) (runs: 257, μ: 32567, ~: 32567)
Suite result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 skipped; finished in 14.13ms (10.92ms CPU time)
```


## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider implementing an allowlist for native node implementations, similar to the vault implementation allowlist, to be managed under the Core owner's authority. And then add performing whiteness validation check of `implementation` from `extraData` parameter in `CoreLib::deployVaults()` or `CoreLib::createVault()` functions.

This allowlist check should also be conducted for `NativeVault::changeNodeImplementation()` function.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L181-L187


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The timestamp validation of `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp` in `validateWithdrawalCredentials` is insufficient and may cause validators to be minted more shares than intended.

## Proof of Concept
This is the validation of the `beaconStateRootProof` timestamp:
```solidity
    if (beaconStateRootProof.timestamp == block.timestamp) {
        revert BeaconTimestampIsCurrent();
    }
    if (
        beaconStateRootProof.timestamp < node.lastSnapshotTimestamp
            || beaconStateRootProof.timestamp < node.currentSnapshotTimestamp
    ) revert BeaconTimestampTooOld();
```

`beaconStateRootProof` is specified by node owners and is used to validate the provided `validatorFieldsProofs` against the beacon block root. The issue is that this validation is insufficient and may allow stale `validatorFieldsProofs` to be valid.

As we can see from EigenLayer's implementation, it is essential that the withdrawal credential proof is not stale as the validator may have been slashed in a more recent beacon state root:
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/bb5ae1822e0444dde1fe95f45cb0d77bf0983436/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L331-L334
```solidity
/**
         * Withdrawal credential proof should not be "stale" (older than VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS) as we are doing a balance check here
         * The validator container persists as the state evolves and even after the validator exits. So we can use a more "fresh" credential proof within
         * the VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS window, not just the first proof where the validator container is registered in the state.
         */
        require(
            oracleTimestamp + VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS >= block.timestamp,
            "EigenPod.verifyWithdrawalCredentials: specified timestamp is too far in past"
        );
```

In the EigenLayer implementation the `oracleTimestamp` variable is the `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp`. It is validated that it is not older than `VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS`:
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/bb5ae1822e0444dde1fe95f45cb0d77bf0983436/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L43-L47
```solidity
    /**
     * @notice Maximum "staleness" of a Beacon Chain state root against which `verifyBalanceUpdate` or `verifyWithdrawalCredentials` may be proven.
     * We can't allow "stale" roots to be used for restaking as the validator may have been slashed in a more updated beacon state root.
     */
    uint256 internal constant VERIFY_BALANCE_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS = 4.5 hours;
```

This validation is missing in the `NativeVault.sol` contract. Furthermore, `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp` in some cases is not even validated as `node.lastSnapshotTimestamp` and `node.currentSnapshotTimestamp` can even be zero if a snapshot is yet to start.

As a result, stale roots may be used to acquire the validator's withdrawal credentials. If a slash on a validator has happened in a more recent beacon state root, the validator will receive more shares of the Native Vault than expected. With more shares, they will be gaining a higher number of rewards unfairly.

Furthermore, it is also important to be aware that in `validateSnapshotProofs` the `snapshot.parentBeaconBlockRoot` that is used to validate the `balanceContainer` may also be stale.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Include a check that `beaconStateRootProof.timestamp` is not older than `4.5 hours` in `validateWithdrawalCredentials`.

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L87-L89
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/entities/HookLib.sol#L55


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In `HookLib.sol` `callHookIfInterfaceImplemented` and `callHook` validate that there is enough gas for the function call to be successful. The issue is that the functions make wrong calculations, which may cause the execution to revert even though, it would have been successful, or not revert when it should have failed. 

In the first case this may prevent users from updating their stake in DSS, initiating and finalizing slashing and configuring operators' registration to DSS. In the second case this will allow malicious operators to bypass the validation, enabling them to execute the [H-02] attack from the Karak Pro League audit: https://code4rena.com/reports/2024-06-karak-pro-league#h-02-malicious-operators-can-bypass-checks-in-dss-hooks

## Proof of Concept
The following validation is made in `callHookIfInterfaceImplemented` and `callHook`:
```solidity
if (gasleft() < (supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)) {
    revert NotEnoughGas();
}
```

Here we can see that in order for a call to be successful `gasleft` needs to be more than `(supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)`.

However, there is a mistake in the calculation, causing it to act unexpectedly. Assuming that `supportsInterfaceGasLimit + hookGasBuffer` is what the rest of the execution will consume, the needed gas will not be `(supportsInterfaceGasLimit * 64 / 63 + hookGasBuffer)`. Instead, the validation should be performed as follows:
```solidity
if (gasleft() < hookGasBuffer || (gasleft() - hookGasBuffer) * 63 / 64 < supportsInterfaceGasLimit) {
    revert NotEnoughGas();
}
```

This is the case as we are assuming that `performLowLevelCallAndLimitReturnData` will consume `hookGasBuffer`. After that in the low-level call `supportsInterfaceGasLimit` needs to be less than or equal to 63/64 of the remaining gas.

# Vulnerability details

### [H-1] Lack of checks allows a `DSS` contract to register as `Operator` to itself

**Description:** According to the contest page "`Operators` perform tasks for the `DSS` in exchange for rewards, and the `DSS` has the ability to `slash` the funds that `Operators` have delegated". Furthermore, a `DSS` has the ability to `Jail` an `Operator` if they have "valid reasons" not to accept a certain `Operator`. I also went through the official docs of Karak and studied the architecture of the protocol of both [v1](https://docs.karak.network/protocol/v1/overview) and [v2](https://docs.karak.network/protocol/v2/dss) and I didn't find any instance where the sponsor mentions that this is deemed as an intended design decision.

Judging based on the architecture of the protocol, the natspec of the `Core::registerOperatorToDSS` function, the official documentation, the contest page, and the Code Walkthrough video that the sponsor provided for C4, I believe it is a reasonable assumption that `DSS` and `Operator` should be two different entities and a `DSS` shouldn't be allowed to register as an `Operator` to itself.

**Impact:** This can be seen as a "conflict of interests". In a normal scenario, the `DSS` would want to reward the `Operators` that perform the tasks that are provided to them, and `slash` or `jail` malicious `Operators` if needed. If a `DSS` is registered as an `Operator` to itself, there is no incentive for the `DSS` to punish the `Operator` as that means that it would punish itself. This also implies that the `Operator` can behave maliciously, because it will never get `slashed` or `jailed`. Furthermore, the `DSS` is allowed to distribute the rewards arbitrarily. Suppose a `DSS` has 10 `Operators` registered, one of them being itself. In that case, it can distribute up to 100% of the rewards back to itself, since it also has the `Operator` role, which will impact the revenue of honest `Operators`.

This doesn't seem to be an intended design choice and even if it was, it may need to be reconsidered because of this conflict of interests.
